# First, the data has to have a shape {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The grammar assumes tidy input

Every mapping we write today — `x=`, `color=`, `size=` — assumes one thing: **each variable you want to map is already a column.**

::: {.gw-box}
Most "I can't make this chart" problems are **data-shape problems**, not plotting problems.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Wide (messy for plotting)**

| name | math | english |
|---|---|---|
| Alice | 90 | 85 |
| Bob | 80 | 78 |

*"subject" is a variable — but it's spread across column headers.*
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Long (tidy)**

| name | subject | score |
|---|---|---|
| Alice | math | 90 |
| Alice | english | 85 |
| Bob | math | 80 |
| Bob | english | 78 |

*Now `subject` is a column you can map.*
:::
:::

## Wickham's three rules {.smaller}

Tidy data (Wickham, *JSS* 2014, [doi:10.18637/jss.v059.i10](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10)):

1. Each **variable** is a column
2. Each **observation** is a row
3. Each **type of observational unit** is a table

```python
df_tidy = df_wide.melt(id_vars="name", var_name="subject", value_name="score")
```

Why this matters beyond neatness:

- **Consistency** — any tidy table works with any grammar-based library
- **Flexibility** — a variable in a column can be mapped to *any* channel
- **Reproducibility** — the same shape ports across pandas, R, SQL

## One tidy table, three questions

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

tidy = pd.DataFrame({
    "year":    [2021, 2022, 2023] * 3,
    "region":  ["North"] * 3 + ["South"] * 3 + ["West"] * 3,
    "sales":   [12, 15, 19, 9, 14, 13, 21, 20, 26],
    "staff":   [4, 5, 6, 3, 5, 4, 7, 7, 8],
})

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.1))
tot = tidy.groupby("region", as_index=False)["sales"].sum()
axes[0].bar(tot["region"], tot["sales"], color="#2E6E8E")
axes[0].set_title("compare categories", fontsize=10)
for r, g in tidy.groupby("region"):
    axes[1].plot(g["year"], g["sales"], marker="o", label=r)
axes[1].set_title("trend over time", fontsize=10)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=7)
axes[2].scatter(tidy["staff"], tidy["sales"], color="#2E6E8E", s=45)
axes[2].set_title("relationship", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Three charts, **one dataframe, zero reshaping**. That is what tidy buys you.

# The grammar of graphics {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Every chart is a mapping

$$\text{data variables} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{visual channels}$$

- **Marks**: points, lines, bars, areas — the geometric objects
- **Channels**: position, length, angle, area, color, shape — the properties that carry data

A "scatter plot" is just: *point marks, two variables on position*. Name the mapping and the chart-type zoo collapses into a system.

## Four components, not two {.smaller}

Marks and channels are only half of it. A full grammar specification also fixes:

| Component | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Marks** | What geometric object? | point, bar, line |
| **Channels** | Which variable to which property? | `x=gdp`, `color=continent` |
| **Coordinates** | What space are marks placed in? | Cartesian, polar, geographic |
| **Scales** | How do data values become channel values? | linear, log, ordinal |

::: {.gw-box}
Change **one** component and you get a different chart — without touching the data.
:::

## Coordinates: the pie chart, explained

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np
vals = [23, 19, 27, 17, 14]
labels = list("ABCDE")

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
ax1 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1)
ax1.bar(labels, vals, color="#2E6E8E")
ax1.set_title("Bar marks, Cartesian coordinates", fontsize=10)

ax2 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2, projection="polar")
theta = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(vals) / sum(vals) * 2 * np.pi])
ax2.bar(theta[:-1], [1] * len(vals), width=np.diff(theta), align="edge",
        color=["#2E6E8E", "#4a89a8", "#6aa4bf", "#9ab8c9", "#c3d5de"])
# label the wedges so the same five categories are traceable across both panels
for lab, t0, t1 in zip(labels, theta[:-1], theta[1:]):
    ax2.text((t0 + t1) / 2, 0.62, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9)
ax2.set_yticks([]); ax2.set_xticks([])
ax2.set_title("Same marks, polar coordinates", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A pie chart **is** a stacked bar chart in polar coordinates. Same data, same marks — one component changed.

## Scales: the axis is a decision

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import plotly.express as px
gap = px.data.gapminder()
g07 = gap[gap["year"] == 2007]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.8, 3.5))
for ax, logx in zip(axes, [False, True]):
    ax.scatter(g07["gdpPercap"], g07["lifeExp"], s=18, alpha=0.65, color="#2E6E8E")
    if logx:
        ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_title("log scale: structure appears" if logx else "linear scale: everything piles up",
                 fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("GDP per capita"); ax.set_ylabel("life expectancy")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Identical data and encoding. **The scale is doing the analytical work** — and it must be labelled, or the reader is misled.

## Four channels at once

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import seaborn as sns
tips = px.data.tips()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.2))
sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="day", style="time", size="size", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("position (x, y) + color (day) + shape (time) + size (party)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Five variables in one chart. Question for the room: **which can you actually read?**

# Perception: not all channels are equal {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Cleveland & McGill (1984)

Showed people the same comparisons encoded differently and **measured decoding error**. The accuracy ranking, top to bottom:

1. **Position** on a common scale
2. Position on non-aligned scales
3. **Length**
4. Angle / slope
5. **Area**
6. Color saturation / volume

::: {.gw-box}
This is why pie charts (angle) lose to bar charts (position/length) for comparison — not taste, **measured human error**.
:::

## See it yourself

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
axes[0].bar(labels, vals, color="#2E6E8E")
axes[0].set_title("Position/length: is C or A bigger? Instant.")
axes[1].pie(vals, labels=labels, startangle=90)
axes[1].set_title("Angle: is B or D bigger? ...slower, less sure.")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Same five numbers. The decoding effort difference is the Cleveland–McGill result, live.

## Color carries two different jobs {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib as mpl
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9.5, 2.2))
cat = plt.get_cmap("tab10")
for i in range(6):
    axes[0].add_patch(mpl.patches.Rectangle((i, 0), 0.92, 1, color=cat(i)))
axes[0].set_xlim(0, 6); axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1); axes[0].axis("off")
axes[0].set_title("Hue → unordered categories (no colour is 'more' than another)", fontsize=9)

seq = plt.get_cmap("Blues")
for i in range(6):
    axes[1].add_patch(mpl.patches.Rectangle((i, 0), 0.92, 1, color=seq(0.15 + i * 0.17)))
axes[1].set_xlim(0, 6); axes[1].set_ylim(0, 1); axes[1].axis("off")
axes[1].set_title("Lightness → ordered magnitude (darker reads as 'more')", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Using **hue** for a quantity implies categories; using **lightness** for categories implies a ranking. Pick the one that matches your variable's type.

[ColorBrewer](https://colorbrewer2.org) exists precisely to make that choice for you — sequential, diverging, qualitative.

## Colour vs. shape for categories

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 40
gx = rng.uniform(0, 10, n * 3); gy = rng.uniform(0, 6, n * 3)
grp = np.repeat([0, 1, 2], n)
cols = ["#2E6E8E", "#d9534f", "#6aa84f"]; marks = ["o", "s", "^"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 2.9))
for k in range(3):
    m = grp == k
    axes[0].scatter(gx[m], gy[m], color=cols[k], s=28)
    axes[1].scatter(gx[m], gy[m], color="#555555", marker=marks[k], s=28)
    axes[2].scatter(gx[m], gy[m], color=cols[k], marker=marks[k], s=28)
for ax, t in zip(axes, ["colour only", "shape only", "colour + shape (redundant)"]):
    ax.set_title(t, fontsize=10); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Colour separates faster; shape survives greyscale printing and colour-blindness. **Redundant encoding** costs a channel but buys robustness.

## When the colormap invents structure

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
gx = np.linspace(0, 1, 300); gy = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
GX, GY = np.meshgrid(gx, gy)
Z = GX + 0.22 * np.sin(5 * GY)          # perfectly smooth, no edges anywhere
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.8, 2.9))
for ax, cm, t in zip(axes, ["jet", "viridis"],
                     ["'jet': bands and edges the data does not contain",
                      "viridis: uniform — reads as the smooth ramp it is"]):
    ax.imshow(Z, cmap=cm, aspect="auto", origin="lower")
    ax.set_title(t, fontsize=9.5); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The underlying field is a **smooth ramp**. Rainbow scales aren't perceptually uniform, so equal steps in data become unequal steps in perceived lightness — inventing boundaries a reader will interpret as real.

Same failure family: **3D bars and pies**, where perspective makes near values look larger than far ones.

## Gestalt: how the eye groups

- **Proximity** — near things read as a group
- **Similarity** — same color/shape reads as a group
- **Enclosure & connection** — boxes and lines bind harder than color
- **Continuity** — the eye follows smooth paths
- **Closure** — the eye completes partial shapes (a dashed outline still reads as a box)

You're already using these (every legend relies on similarity). Design = using them **on purpose**.

## Preattentive features

Some properties pop out **before** conscious attention — in < 250 ms, regardless of how many distractors:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
xs, ys = rng.uniform(0, 10, 60), rng.uniform(0, 4, 60)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 2.8))
ax.scatter(xs, ys, color="#9ab8c9", s=60)
ax.scatter([6.2], [2.1], color="#d9534f", s=90)
ax.set_title("You found the red dot before you decided to look for it.")
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Color, size, orientation — and **motion**, the strongest of all, which is why a single animated element will dominate an interactive dashboard whether you meant it to or not.

**One** popout works; several at once cancel each other.

# Expressiveness & effectiveness {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Two rules for choosing encodings {.smaller}

**Expressiveness** — the encoding should show *all and only* the data's structure:

- Don't encode an unordered category on an ordered channel (a rainbow for species implies an order that doesn't exist)

**Effectiveness** — put the *most important* variable on the *most accurate* channel:

- The variable your reader must compare precisely → **position**
- Grouping/context variables → color, shape

::: {.gw-box}
These two rules + the accuracy ranking = a *procedure* for designing a chart. No memorized chart types required.
:::

## Cost of a wrong channel

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
sub = tips.groupby("day", as_index=False)["tip"].mean()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
axes[0].bar(sub["day"], sub["tip"], color="#2E6E8E")
axes[0].set_title("Comparison variable on POSITION: differences obvious")
axes[1].scatter([1]*len(sub), range(len(sub)), s=sub["tip"]*900, color="#2E6E8E", alpha=0.7)
for i, (d, t) in enumerate(zip(sub["day"], sub["tip"])):
    axes[1].annotate(d, (1.02, i), fontsize=9, va="center")
axes[1].set_title("Same data on AREA: can you rank them?")
axes[1].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

# Reading a chart critically {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The truncated axis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
q = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"]; v = [98, 99, 101, 103]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.3))
axes[0].bar(q, v, color="#d9534f"); axes[0].set_ylim(97, 104)
axes[0].set_title("y starts at 97: 'explosive growth'", fontsize=10)
axes[1].bar(q, v, color="#2E6E8E"); axes[1].set_ylim(0, 110)
axes[1].set_title("y starts at 0: a 5% drift", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Identical numbers. With **bar marks, length encodes value** — so the baseline must be zero, or the encoding lies. (For line marks on a common scale, truncation can be legitimate.)

## Three questions for any chart

**1. What is actually being compared?** — name the marks and the channel carrying the comparison.

**2. Are the scales honest?** — zero baseline for length; log scales labelled; consistent axes across small multiples.

**3. Does the encoding match the variable type?** — ordered channel for ordered data, unordered for categories.

::: {.gw-box}
These are the same three rules you just learned, run **backwards** — as a reader instead of an author.
:::
